doc.title: Chris Parker interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, January 5, 2023

title: Click tracks and movie soundtracks: Steelyard Blues and Morricone
summary: He discusses clicks and tempo in pop sessions, then film work on Steelyard Blues and conducting by Ennio Morricone on The Untouchables.

story.theme_name: Jazz musicians in the movies and film scoring
story.community_name: Jazz musicians on film and studio scoring

blocks.x: You’ve also played on a lot of movie soundtracks.
Was that the first time that you had used a click track or are some records made that some of the pop records you’ve done, did you have a click track in your headphones?

Yeah it depends on the artists. Some people if they don’t, if they wrote the song with the drum machine pattern or some groove they came up with on a keyboard or something like that so we’d play along to that and maybe in the studio kind of pare it down to just the cowbell or just a click or sometimes they come in with a tempo in mind and sing it at that tempo but when recording starts you know they get excited or they lose that initial feel. So I’m always very careful to take a reading kind of when we run it down the first time. I bring a metronome and take a reading on the Metronome where we are right now, this first rundown where the singer is comfortable, the red light is not on yet, this is where it feels good to them. Make a note of that marking and maybe later in the session somebody, “Geez it’s not feeling good, it feels nervous, it doesn’t have the energy it had.” And I say, “Let’s go back to the original tempo, what do you mean?” Well the original tempo was 112 BPM let’s try it back there, you know and you realize they’re up around 132 and wondering why it doesn’t have the same groovy feel that it had. Sometimes, I mean the movies, they were up until — I don’t know if they still use SMPTE but you have to be with the click because it’s frame by frame, at least in the old days, so that was a different thing. But one of the first movies I did was with Paul Butterfield and Nick Gravenites and Mike Bloomfield called “Steelyard Blues” with Jane Fonda and Donald Sutherland and that was, they wrote songs for the movie and we watched the movie as we were playing the songs and sometimes the director would say, you know, “It needs a little edge on it” or “hold it back a little so that the song doesn’t end before the scene ends.” Little adjustments like that. There was no click, there was no SMPTE there was just the director and a big video monitor and you’re watching the movie go by. Same thing with Ennio Morricone doing “Untouchables.” You know there was a click but he wasn’t paying attention to it. He was watching the movie go by and conducting as the scene went by so you had to really watch him and stay with him as a
conductor to make sure that it came out right. And then they underdubbed SMPTE and whatever else they needed to do the editing later.

Well Ennio Morricone was fabulous you know. Beautiful composer and a beautiful human being and he had done this for years, and he was a trumpet player in Rome for years so he really knew the studio and knew what musicians were capable of and he had a beautiful Italian woman translating for him to the orchestra and he would sometimes send her to the drum booth, you know, to tell me to have a fantasy, you know, loosen up and feel romantic. And a couple of times I sort of played possum, “Gee what should I do here?” You know so he would have to send the translator into the drum booth.
You got to have a short visit.
Yeah. Tell me again what I should be doing here. That was the “Untouchables” that movie which has got some amazing scenes in it.
